exercises.title: Two statements, one circuit
exercises.brief:
Build and3, whose output is the and of all three inputs, using two continuous assignments and one internal wire. The checker proves it against a & b & c.

The starter writes the two lines in the order a program would need. Leave them in that order. The bug is in one of the expressions, not in where it sits.
exercises.concept: A continuous assignment is a permanent connection, so the line that drives a wire may be written after the line that reads it.
hints: Read what t is connected to, then read what y is connected to, and ask which input never reaches the output.

diagnose.prose: The solver found inputs where your module and a & b & c disagree. One of the three inputs is not wired into the result at all: follow y back through t and see which letter never appears.
Read the line the parser names. Every continuous assignment needs assign, and every internal signal needs a wire declaration before something drives it.

exercises.after: The order of the two lines never mattered. Swap them and synthesise again: the same two gates, because a circuit has no first line.

spec.gold: module gold(input a, input b, input c, output y); assign y = a & b & c; endmodule

exercises.title: Two things soldered to one wire
exercises.brief:
The starter drives y twice, once from each of the two functions it was meant to choose between. Synthesise it and read what the tool says.

Fix it by driving y once, from a selection between the two, using s. When s is 0 the output is the and, and when s is 1 it is the or.
exercises.concept: A wire is a node with one driver, and two continuous assignments to the same name describe two gate outputs soldered together.
hints: One assignment, and the choice goes inside the expression.

diagnose.prose: The tool names the signal that two things drive. Nothing here is an override: the second assignment does not replace the first, because there is no first. Both connections exist at once, which is a short circuit in copper and an error here.
One driver now, and it selects the wrong way round. s at 0 should give the and.

exercises.after: The rule is the one from the shared bus in Part II, enforced at build time instead of by smoke. A synthesiser can catch it because it can see every driver at once, which is exactly what a wire being a node rather than a variable means.

spec.gold: module gold(input a, input b, input s, output y); assign y = s ? (a | b) : (a & b); endmodule

exercises.title: A swap needs no temporary
exercises.brief:
Build swap, where x follows b and y follows a.

In a program this needs a third variable, because the first assignment destroys what the second one wanted to read. Here it does not, and the starter is what the programmer's habit produces.
exercises.concept: Nothing is destroyed by a connection, so the sequencing that a software swap needs has nothing to sequence.
hints: Each output is connected to an input. Say which, and write those two connections.

diagnose.prose: Follow the wires. The starter connects x to a, then connects y to x, which is the same node, so both outputs carry a and b never leaves the module. Reading a wire does not consume it, and writing one does not happen at a moment, so the temporary has nothing to protect.

exercises.after: Two wires crossing. There is no third gate and no instant at which the old value is at risk, which is the difference between a connection and an assignment stated as compactly as it can be.

spec.gold: module gold(input a, input b, output x, output y); assign x = b; assign y = a; endmodule

exercises.title: What cannot change is not built
exercises.brief:
Build mask, whose output is a unchanged. Write it as a combined with a constant, so that the expression contains a gate and the result does not.

The budget is zero cells. Anything that survives the optimiser fails.
exercises.concept: The optimiser deletes what cannot change, so a cell count reports what you asked for rather than what you typed.
hints: Which constant makes an and gate do nothing? Which one makes an or gate do nothing?

diagnose.prose: The output is a constant rather than a, so the solver finds an input where you disagree. a & 1'b0 is always 0 and a | 1'b1 is always 1: you picked the constant that wins the expression instead of the one that yields to it.

Correct now, and a cell survived. Something in the expression still depends on more than a, so there is real logic left for the optimiser to keep. The identity you want folds all the way down to a plain wire.
Read the line the parser names. A one-bit constant is written 1'b0 or 1'b1.

exercises.after: Zero cells for a line that clearly contains a gate. This is why the report is worth more than your reading of the source, and it is also why a design can silently be smaller than intended: the tool deletes an unused output with exactly the same enthusiasm.

spec.gold: module gold(input a, output y); assign y = a; endmodule

exercises.title: The carry falls out in the middle
exercises.brief:
Build add4, a four-bit adder whose five-bit output holds the sum including the carry.

The starter computes the sum into an internal wire and then widens it. Both lines look reasonable. The result is wrong for a third of the input pairs.
exercises.concept: Width is decided where an expression is evaluated, not where its result eventually lands.
hints: The addition has to be five bits wide at the moment it is performed.

diagnose.prose: The solver names an input pair where you disagree with a + b, and it will be one where the sum exceeds 15. The starter adds at the width of t, which is four bits, so the carry is discarded before the widening to five bits ever happens. Widening afterwards cannot recover a bit that was already dropped.
Read the line the parser names. A vector is declared as wire [4:0] name;.

exercises.after: Assigning straight to the five-bit output makes the addition five bits wide, because the width of a continuous assignment is decided by the widest thing in it, including the left side. The intermediate wire was not a step along the way, it was a narrower circuit.

spec.gold: module gold(input [3:0] a, input [3:0] b, output [4:0] s); assign s = a + b; endmodule

exercises.title: A loop is four gates, not four passes
exercises.brief:
Build parity4, whose output is the exclusive or of all four bits of a.

Write it with a for loop. There is no counter in the result: the tool unrolls the loop while elaborating and emits the gates side by side.
exercises.concept: A loop bound has to be known at build time because it decides how many copies of the body exist, and hardware cannot change how much of itself there is.
hints: Four bits means four terms. Count how many the starter's bounds actually produce.

diagnose.prose: The solver disagrees with you on an input where the bit you skipped is 1. Count the iterations: the starter's condition stops one short, so one of the four gates is never emitted and that bit of a reaches nothing.
Read the line the parser names. A for loop that assigns needs to sit inside an always @* block, and the target has to be declared reg.

exercises.after: Four XOR gates, all of which exist at once and settle together. Change the bound to eight and you have eight gates and a longer path to settle, which is the sense in which a loop here is a multiplier rather than a cost you pay once.

spec.gold: module gold(input [3:0] a, output y); assign y = ^a; endmodule

exercises.title: The carry chain, one stage at a time
exercises.brief:
Build ripple4 structurally: four full adder stages, each taking the carry the previous stage produced.

The starter wires every stage's carry input to the module's cin. Each stage is correct on its own and the whole thing is wrong, which is the failure a structural description makes easy to write and easy to see.
exercises.concept: Instances are separate hardware, so what connects them is the only thing that makes a chain a chain.
hints: Stage 1 needs the carry that stage 0 produced, not the one the module was given.

diagnose.prose: The solver names inputs where you disagree with a + b + cin, and the smallest one will be a pair that carries out of bit 0. Every stage in the starter is handed the same carry, so a carry generated inside the adder never travels. The chain is the wiring, not the stages.
Read the line the parser names. An instance is name inst (.port(signal), ...) with a semicolon.

exercises.after: This is the adder from Part II with the same carry path and the same worst case, where bit 0 decides bit 3 and every stage between them has to settle in order. Unit 016 measures what that costs.

spec.gold: module gold(input [3:0] a, input [3:0] b, input cin, output [3:0] s, output cout); assign {cout, s} = a + b + cin; endmodule

exercises.title: Instantiating is copying
exercises.brief:
Build maj3, high when at least two of the three inputs are.

Use three instances of and2, one per pair, and combine them. The starter uses one instance and reads its output twice, which is what calling a function would do and is not what an instance is.
exercises.concept: An instance is a piece of the chip rather than a call, so using one twice is not sharing hardware, it is reading one wire twice.
hints: Three pairs need three gates. There is no way to make one gate produce two different answers at the same instant.

diagnose.prose: The starter feeds a and b into the single instance and then treats its output as though it also meant b & c. One gate has one output and that output has one value, so two of the three terms are the same term. Three pairs need three instances.
Correct, and larger than three and-gates plus the combining logic. Check that you have not instantiated more gates than the three pairs need.
Read the line the parser names. Every instance needs its own name.

exercises.after: Three instances, three gates, three times the area. Sharing one gate between the pairs is possible, but it costs a multiplexer to choose its inputs and a register to keep the earlier answer, and it takes three clock cycles. That trade has a name, and Part V spends most of its time on it.

spec.gold: module gold(input a, input b, input c, output y); assign y = (a & b) | (b & c) | (a & c); endmodule
